The Blue-crowned hanging parrot (Loriculus galgulus) is a small, frugivorous parrot inhabiting the lowland forests of Southeast Asia. Eggs incubated at a temperature of 30 °C [T = 30 °C] require approximately 21 days [ab = approximately 21 days] to hatch, a developmental period that is relatively brief and consistent with the altricial mode typical of psittaciforms. Upon hatching, the altricial nestlings exhibit a remarkably low neonatal body mass, with newly hatched chicks weighing just 3.9 grams [Ww0 = 3.9 grams]. This initial mass is a very small fraction of the size the chick will eventually attain, and it underscores the complete dependence of the hatchling on parental brooding and provisioning during the critical first days of life.

Females of this species ultimately reach an adult body mass of 28 grams [Wwi = 28 grams], placing them among the smaller members of the parrot family. This ultimate wet weight for females falls within the broader documented range of 22 to 35 grams for the species and is associated with a slow pace of life. Under the typical thermal conditions of its active metabolic state (41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]), the nestling period is relatively short; the estimated time since birth at fledging is approximately 35 days [tx = approximately 35 days]. This rapid developmental trajectory from a helpless chick to a flight-capable juvenile allows the brood to vacate the nest cavity before the onset of heavy monsoon rains.

The attainment of sexual maturity in this species occurs after a prolonged juvenile phase. Puberty is reached at approximately 105 days [tp = approximately 105 days] after hatching, a duration that reflects the considerable time required for somatic growth and organ maturation in a bird that will eventually breed in the at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C] forest canopy. This milestone marks the onset of gonadal activity, though actual breeding is typically deferred further. The relatively late puberty, when considered alongside the low neonate mass, highlights a life-history strategy that prioritizes extended parental investment in a few, well-provisioned offspring.

First reproduction is substantially delayed beyond the point of sexual maturation. Under favorable captive conditions maintained at 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], the time since birth at first brood is approximately 657 days [tR = approximately 657 days], meaning that most females do not lay their first clutch until nearly two years of age. This prolonged interval between hatching and first successful reproduction is characteristic of slow-living avian species that face low extrinsic adult mortality rates. During this pre-reproductive period, young parrots refine foraging skills, establish dominance hierarchies, and, in the wild, secure a suitable nesting hollow.

The maximum recorded lifespan for this species is approximately 3,759 days [am = approximately 3,759 days] when maintained at 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], which equates to just over ten years. This longevity is substantial for a bird of such modest body size. The basal metabolic rate, measured under post-absorptive thermoneutral conditions, is 93 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 93 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], a value that reflects the elevated energetic costs of maintaining endothermy. In terms of annual reproductive effort, the maximum reproduction rate is approximately 3.5 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 3.5 offspring per year], expressed as females producing 3 to 4 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 3 to 4 eggs per clutch], with a single clutch laid each year [F_R_i = single clutch laid each year], a modest output that aligns with the species extended parental care period and low fecundity.
